title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 15: The Judiciary and the Economy
keywords: a friend rather than a foe of legitimate business
full control and supervision of the State
Department of Environment and Natural Resources
justice and jobs, freedom and food
primary_topics: Chapter 15 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- CJP's address to a mining conference explaining the Philippine judiciary's place in the economy: how the Constitution structures the three branches, why the courts' duty to strike down grave abuse of discretion exists, and why a well-functioning judiciary is indispensable to a sound business climate.

An answer to three recurring business complaints he has heard here and abroad -- that the Supreme Court unduly interferes in business, that it reviews the wisdom of the other branches' acts, and what its stand is on public contracts -- concluding that the Court is 'a friend rather than a foe of legitimate business.'

A practical primer for foreign mining investors on the constitutional modes of participation: FTAAs with 100-percent foreign-owned companies entered into only with the President, co-production, joint-venture and mineral-production-sharing agreements with up to 40 percent foreign equity, exploration permits, and the rule that the Constitution and laws are read into every contract.

The closing reaffirmation of his judicial philosophy: that courts must not only safeguard liberty but also nurture prosperity, so that the Court espouses justice and jobs, freedom and food, integrity and investments.
sub_topics: The constitutional setting: a Constitution crafted after a dictatorial regime was toppled in the bloodless 1986 People Power Revolution, with a government republican in nature and presidential in form, and powers shared among Congress, the President and the Supreme Court.

Separation of powers as a device against concentrated authority, with the branches neither antagonistic nor subservient but coordinating and checking one another -- a feature CJP says differentiates the Philippines from many countries in the region.

The judiciary's structure: a centralized and unitary Judicial Department with a single Supreme Court performing the functions that constitutional, administrative and commercial tribunals perform elsewhere, above the Court of Appeals, Court of Tax Appeals and Sandiganbayan, the regional trial courts and the metropolitan and municipal trial courts.

The express mandate to nullify any act of any branch or official, including the President or Congress, done with grave abuse of discretion -- a 'duty,' not merely a power, written into the Constitution after the Martial Law years to make the courts 'activists' capable of checking the political branches.

The business premise: investor confidence is tied to a stable and predictable justice system, a point CJP says makes perfect sense to a former business executive like himself, and one raised in his recent meetings with business leaders in New York, Washington DC and the United Kingdom.

First question -- undue interference in business: commercial transactions have been sources of litigation for more than a century, from sales, leases, construction and interest rates to natural-resource agreements, and now patents, copyright, new communications methods, genetically modified organisms, in vitro fertilization and cloning.

The reductio he presses: if courts were excluded from deciding economic questions, who else would settle them, under what standards, and who would protect parties and the public from economic tyrannies, excesses and abuses.

His book 'Leveling the Playing Field' (2004) invoked for the proposition that the judiciary exists to level the playing field for business under the rule of law and that the same principle of fairness applies to contracts and economic transactions.

Decisions annulling electricity-rate increases and nullifying public contracts defended as not anathema to private investment: the Constitution recognizes the indispensable role of the private sector, but contracts violating the Constitution or the laws enjoy neither protection nor sanctity, and nullifications are the exception rather than the rule.

Second question -- review of wisdom: the answer is no; the Court does not take up matters reserved to the people in their sovereign capacity or delegated to the full discretionary authority of the political branches, and in case of doubt upholds the constitutionality of legislative and executive acts.

The Mining Act of 1995 ruling quoted as the Court's own statement of restraint -- it 'declares what the Constitution and the laws say, interprets only when necessary, and refrains from delving into matters of policy' -- and the same laissez-faire posture in reviewing purely private commercial contracts under the parties' freedom to stipulate.

Third question -- public contracts: extra vigilance where a government agency is a party or public funds are spent, and special care in litigation involving corruption and opaqueness, because the constitutional duty to strike down grave abuse cannot be evaded.

Nullification without supremacy: when the Court voids executive or legislative action it merely sees to it that the Constitution and the laws override the desires and caprices of officials, since the rule of law, not of individuals, must prevail.

Three pieces of practical advice to investors -- abide by the laws and regulations; engage ethical, competent and credible lawyers before rather than after contracting; and avoid transactions requiring bribery, bearing in mind the Anti-Money Laundering Act (RA 9160) and its identification, record-keeping and reporting requirements.

Foreign mining participation under Section 2 of Article XII: FTAAs for large-scale exploration, development and utilization of minerals, petroleum and mineral oils, entered into by 100-percent foreign-owned companies only with the President; forests, fisheries and lands are not fit subjects; small-scale mining is reserved to Filipinos.

The alternative vehicles -- CPAs, JVAs and MPSAs with up to 40 percent foreign equity -- and how each allocates inputs, exclusive rights, equity and shares in gross output, with no limitation as to resource or project size except small-scale mining.

Exploration permits: the right to explore but not to extract and carry off minerals, convertible into an MPSA, JVA, CPA or FTAA, serving to protect the grantee's interests during the costly pre-revenue period.

Constitution and laws read into every mining agreement: EDU remains subject to the 'full control and supervision of the State,' exercised by the President and the DENR secretary as alter ego, and while courts will not inordinately interfere with the presidential prerogative to fix the sharing of net mining revenues, they may nullify FTAA provisions that surrender or dilute state control or are grossly disadvantageous to the nation.

The judiciary as the last bulwark of democracy and ultimate recourse for grievances, with World Bank East Asia and Pacific counsel Anthony Gerald Toft quoted on the Philippine Supreme Court's pivotal constitutional position and its standing as a key element of checks and balances.

The closing: the Court as a friend, not a foe, of investors whose rights are trampled by anyone -- competitor, erstwhile partner, or the highest official -- and the philosophy of Liberty and Prosperity that pairs justice with jobs and democracy with development.

stances.claim: The Supreme Court does not unduly interfere in business: commercial transactions have been ordinary subjects of litigation for more than a century, and excluding economic questions from judicial review would leave no one to protect parties and the public from economic tyrannies, excesses and abuses.
stances.rhetorical_move: reductio ad absurdum plus historical record: asking who else would decide such cases and under what standards, after listing a century of commercial litigation and the new questions of the information and bio-scientific ages

stances.claim: The Court does not review the wisdom of the political branches' acts; as a rule it respects them, and in case of doubt upholds the constitutionality of legislative and executive acts.
stances.rhetorical_move: self-citation of the Court's own holding: quoting the Mining Act ruling that the Court 'refrains from delving into matters of policy' as proof of institutional restraint

stances.claim: Striking down grave abuse of discretion is a duty and not merely a power, so the Court cannot shirk it -- especially where a government agency is a party, public funds are spent, or corruption and opaqueness are in issue.
stances.rhetorical_move: power/duty distinction stated as an aphorism -- a power can be relinquished, a duty cannot be evaded -- to foreclose any expectation of judicial abstention in public contracts

stances.claim: Investors have nothing to fear from the Court's power to nullify contracts if they abide by the law, retain ethical and competent counsel before contracting, and avoid transactions requiring bribery.
stances.rhetorical_move: conditional reassurance turned into practical advice: three numbered rules, each with a proverb or statute attached, that shift risk from the Court's power to the investor's own conduct

stances.claim: Judicial nullification does not make the Court superior to the President and Congress; it merely ensures that the Constitution and the laws override the desires and caprices of officials.
stances.rhetorical_move: disclaiming supremacy while defending the power: recasting judicial review as service to the rule of law rather than assertion of hierarchy

notable_anecdotes: CJP invokes his own past as a business executive to explain why the link between investor confidence and a stable, predictable justice system 'makes perfect sense' to him.
He reports that the same recurring questions about judicial interference were put to him in recent meetings with business leaders in New York, Washington DC and the United Kingdom.

He counsels investors to ask friends for recommendations of reputable lawyers, noting the difference between a lawyer whose practice is murky and one whose practice is aboveboard, and that lawyers with an ethical compass see the legal pitfalls more clearly.

He recounts the recent visit of Anthony Gerald Toft, the World Bank's counsel for East Asia and the Pacific, who called the Philippine Supreme Court a pivotal constitutional institution and a key element of the system of checks and balances.

He recalls that the framers, learning from the Martial Law years begun in 1972, deliberately made the courts 'activists' by increasing their powers and duties so the executive and legislative wielders of power could be effectively checked.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 15 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduces Chief Justice Panganiban's address on the judiciary and the economy, delivered to an audience that included delegates to the 6th Mining Conference. He began with the constitutional setting: a charter crafted after the bloodless 1986 People Power Revolution, a republican and presidential government whose powers are shared among Congress, the President and a single, unitary Supreme Court, with the branches coordinating and checking one another. He stressed the courts' express mandate to nullify any act of any branch or official done with grave abuse of discretion -- a duty written in after the Martial Law years to make the courts 'activists' capable of checking the political branches -- and argued that a well-functioning judiciary is indispensable to a sound business climate because investor confidence is tied to a stable and predictable justice system. He then answered three recurring business complaints. To the charge of undue interference he replied that commercial transactions have been litigated for more than a century and now include patents, copyright, genetically modified organisms and cloning, and asked who else would decide such questions or protect the public from economic tyrannies; citing his book 'Leveling the Playing Field,' he maintained that the Court is 'a friend rather than a foe of legitimate business' and that nullifications of contracts are exceptions. To the charge of reviewing the wisdom of other branches he answered no, quoting the Mining Act of 1995 ruling that the Court 'refrains from delving into matters of policy,' and noted the same laissez-faire posture toward purely private contracts. On public contracts he said the Court is extra vigilant where public funds or corruption are involved, because a power can be relinquished but a duty cannot be evaded, while insisting that nullification asserts the rule of law rather than judicial supremacy. He advised investors to obey the law, hire ethical counsel before contracting, and avoid bribery under RA 9160, then explained FTAAs, CPAs, JVAs, MPSAs and exploration permits, the reservation of small-scale mining to Filipinos, and the State's full control and supervision. Quoting World Bank counsel Anthony Gerald Toft, he closed on a judiciary that espouses justice and jobs, freedom and food, integrity and investments.
